clue.text: Poultry and moussaka? Oddly, nothing after

indicators.note: after places the word for nothing behind the odd letters of the dish
oddly asks for the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of the dish named just before it

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket

explanation.surface: A diner looks at a plate of poultry and moussaka and finds nothing left.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd letters of MOUSSAKA give MUSK. The question mark and comma break the clue in odd places: 'Oddly' belongs with moussaka, not with the poultry.
explanation.definitionFit: A musk duck is a species of waterfowl, and ducks kept for the table count as poultry.

clue.text: Drama in posh part of London, reported by Cockney woman

indicators.note: the place name is to be said in a Cockney accent, where the vowel of the first syllable shifts

parts.note: Mayfair is an expensive district of central London
a lady is a woman

explanation.surface: A Cockney woman reports some drama going on in a smart London district.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney accent is said to turn MAY into something close to MY, so 'Mayfair' becomes MY FAIR. The musical itself is about a Cockney flower girl, Eliza Doolittle.
explanation.definitionFit: The stage musical about Eliza Doolittle is a drama, here loosely standing for any stage play.

clue.text: Stopped dead-end kids also taking pennies at checkout

indicators.note: the end of the word kids is wanted, its final letter only

parts.note: also means too
d is the old abbreviation for a penny, so pennies are Ds
a till is where a shop's checkout takes the money

explanation.surface: Youngsters from a deprived background also pocket a few coins at a supermarket checkout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead-end kids' reads like slum children, but only the end of 'kids', S, is used. D for penny comes from the pre-decimal British currency, where d stood for a penny.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand still is to stop moving entirely, so the past form matches stopped.

clue.text: Dead-end pub serves these parts of Yorkshire

parts.note: the end of the word dead is its last letter, D
a pub serves ales, kinds of beer

explanation.surface: A run-down pub serves visitors in the Yorkshire countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: The Yorkshire Dales are the valleys and uplands of northern England's Yorkshire, a large county. 'These' does double duty in the surface but the wordplay reads 'pub serves these' as ALES.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dales are valleys forming a well-known upland region of Yorkshire in northern England.

clue.text: Boat in canal, rot swirling in contrasting motion

indicators.note: in places the boat inside the jumbled letters of the other two words
swirling suggests the letters of canal and rot being churned into a new order

parts.note: a punt is a flat-bottomed boat

explanation.surface: A boat sits on a canal where rotting debris swirls around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swirling' rearranges CANAL ROT around the boat; 'Boat' is not the setter's name here but the punt itself, and counterpoint is the musical term behind the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Counterpoint sets independent melodic lines against one another, often moving in contrary directions, which is what the musical adjective describes.

clue.text: Boatman's settled in dead-end street or strip

indicators.note: settled in places the setter's contraction inside the end letter and the street abbreviation

parts.note: the end of the word dead is its last letter, D
Boatman is the setter, so Boatman's means the setter has, written I've

explanation.surface: The setter has moved into a dead-end street, or perhaps a strip of land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boatman's' stands for 'Boatman has', and from the setter's own mouth that is I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: To divest is to strip someone of clothing, property or office.

clue.text: Showing no concern for four in dead end

indicators.note: in puts the Roman numeral inside the word for a dead end

parts.note: an impasse is a dead end, a situation with no way forward
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in a dead end shows no concern for the four people with them.
explanation.definitionFit: Impassive describes a face or manner that betrays no emotion or concern.

clue.text: Head over heels, aching for love

indicators.note: head over heels means turned upside down, so in a down entry the word is read upward

parts.note: aching means sore

explanation.surface: Someone head over heels in love is aching for their beloved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head over heels' looks like part of the romance, but it is the signal to turn SORE upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of love, and his name stands for erotic love itself.

clue.text: International meeting set up on time

indicators.note: up turns the word set over, reading upward in this down entry

explanation.surface: An international meeting is set up on time.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test is a full international cricket or rugby match, so 'meeting' means a sporting fixture, not a conference.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket and rugby a Test is a full international match between two countries.

clue.text: Part of verse has line with something missing: gravity — it's lightweight

parts.note: a foot is a metrical unit, part of a line of verse

indicators.note: with something missing says the word for line loses a letter, here its last

parts.note: line is the word itself before trimming
g is the symbol for acceleration due to gravity

explanation.surface: Part of a poem has a line short, and the gravity of the piece is slight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with something missing' trims LINE to LIN. The setter's link 'it's' introduces the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Footling means trivial or of no importance, much as lightweight does of a person or argument.

clue.text: Spirits of dead-end kids: rebellious, outspoken, tuneless

indicators.note: end asks for the final letter of kids
rebellious suggests letters breaking ranks, so outspoken is rearranged once some are gone

parts.note: tuneless means the letters of tune are taken out of the pool

explanation.surface: Children from a deprived area are rebellious, outspoken and can't sing in tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebellious' and 'tuneless' together take TUNE from OUTSPOKEN, leaving OSPOK, which is rearranged to POOKS. Only 'end' of 'dead-end' is in the wordplay; 'of dead' is padding that keeps the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Spooks are ghosts, and ghosts are spirits of the dead.

clue.text: A classy purée, ordered with bream etc

indicators.note: ordered suggests the letters being put into a new arrangement, like dishes on a menu

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, the accent ignored

explanation.surface: A diner orders a smart purée to go with bream and other fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' looks like a diner's choice but rearranges A CLASSY PURÉE. The definition is loose: the sauce is a classic accompaniment to fish such as bream.
explanation.definitionFit: This green herb sauce is traditionally served with fish, so it comes with bream and similar dishes.

clue.text: Perhaps stocks of Lada Ltd in Russia unreliable

indicators.note: unreliable hints that the company's letters cannot be trusted to stay in place

parts.note: Ltd taken as written, the abbreviation for limited company
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Shares in the Russian carmaker Lada are risky investments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unreliable' scrambles LTD IN RUSSIA. Lada, the Russian car brand, is surface colour only.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrials are shares in manufacturing companies, so they are an example of stocks.

clue.text: Boatman at helm of tug gets a good deal (after inflation)

indicators.note: after puts the good deal behind the inflation measure

parts.note: rive is an archaic word meaning to tear or pull, so to tug
RPI, the Retail Price Index, is the UK measure of inflation
a lot means a good deal

explanation.surface: A boatman in charge of a tug gets a decent pay rise once inflation is counted.
explanation.walkthrough: RPI is the British Retail Price Index, the old headline inflation figure. 'Boatman' is also the setter's own name.
explanation.definitionFit: A river pilot guides vessels along a river, so is one kind of boatman.

clue.text: Attacked with hammer in deserted complex

indicators.note: complex suggests the letters of in deserted tangled into a new structure

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone was assaulted with a hammer in an abandoned building complex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complex' looks like a building, but it scrambles IN DESERTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat is tenderised by pounding it with a mallet, so it is beaten with a hammer.

clue.text: Dead-end career next?

parts.note: the late Mr X is a dead man, so late means dead

indicators.note: end asks for the final letter of career

explanation.surface: Someone in a job going nowhere wonders what comes next.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead-end' is split: 'Dead' gives LATE and 'end' takes the R from 'career'.
explanation.definitionFit: Later means afterwards or subsequently, what comes next; the question mark flags the loose sense.

clue.text: Measure of liquidity in climate of anger about bank sitting on gold

indicators.note: about places the word for anger around the bank and the metal symbol

parts.note: rage is anger

indicators.note: sitting on puts the bank above the metal in this down entry

parts.note: ING is a Dutch banking group
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: In an angry financial climate, a bank props up its liquidity with gold reserves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liquidity' and 'bank' sound financial, but the liquid here is rainfall. ING is a Dutch bank.
explanation.definitionFit: A rain gauge collects and records rainfall, measuring the wet side of a climate.

clue.text: Pressure-formed, it's de-ice spray for farmers

parts.note: p is the symbol for pressure in physics

indicators.note: formed suggests the letters following being shaped into something new

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
taken as written without the hyphen

explanation.surface: A pressurised de-icing spray is offered to farmers.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'Pressure-formed' disguises two pieces: P, then 'formed' rearranging IT'S DE-ICE into ESTICIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmers spray pesticide on crops to kill insects and other pests.

clue.text: Flirting with dead-end relationship

parts.note: the end of the word dead is its last letter, D
an alliance is a relationship or association

explanation.surface: Someone flirts while trapped in a relationship going nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Dalliance is casual flirtation or a brief romantic involvement, so it means flirting.

clue.text: Polish anthem endures in the heart

indicators.note: in the heart says the letters sit in the middle of the words anthem endures

explanation.surface: The Polish national anthem lives on in people's hearts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like a nationality, but it is the verb to polish a text.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct and improve it, which is to polish it.

clue.text: Almost catches customer: not exactly cricket

indicators.note: almost says the word for catches stops short of its full length

parts.note: grasps means catches or seizes
a shopper is a customer

explanation.surface: A fielder nearly takes catches, but it is not quite the game of cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims GRASPS to GRAS. 'Not exactly cricket' looks like 'not fair play', but the answer is an insect like a cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A grasshopper is a close relative of the cricket, a similar jumping insect but not the same one.

clue.text: Charge out non-resident's take-away dinners

indicators.note: out signals the letters of the guest are to be reordered after the removal

parts.note: taken as written, without apostrophe or hyphen
dinners gives the letters that are removed from the pool

explanation.surface: A hotel charges a non-resident for takeaway dinners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take-away' tells you to remove DINNERS from NON-RESIDENT'S, leaving N, O, E, S, T, which 'out' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is an attack or assault, the same as a charge in battle.

clue.text: Letters written in dead-end Middle East port

indicators.note: letters written in points to a run of letters found inside the next word

explanation.surface: Correspondence is sent to a Middle East port that seems a dead end.
explanation.definitionFit: Aden is a port city in Yemen, on the Gulf of Aden in the Middle East.

clue.text: Ill-mannered about dead-end street in Paris

indicators.note: about puts the French street around the letter from the end of dead

parts.note: rue is French for street
the end of the word dead is its last letter, D

explanation.surface: Someone is rude about a cul-de-sac in Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: Rude means ill-mannered or impolite.

clue.text: Gather for a drink after day is done

indicators.note: after places the drink behind the day abbreviation

parts.note: rum is a drink
up means finished or done, as in time is up

explanation.surface: People get together for a drink once the working day is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' and 'for a' are links joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To drum up support or business is to gather it through effort.

clue.text: Drama of dead-end soul-searching wrongly denying anger

indicators.note: wrongly says the remaining letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written without the hyphen
anger gives letters that are denied, taken out of the pool

explanation.surface: A play about introspection that wrongly refuses to admit any anger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'denying anger' removes ANGER from SOUL-SEARCHING, leaving SOULSCHI, which 'wrongly' rearranges. Sartre's play is known in English as No Exit, hence 'dead-end'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sartre's play is set in a closed room in hell with no exit, a literal dead end.

clue.text: Shocking Scene One from brother's production of "Three Sisters"?

indicators.note: shocking suggests the letters of scene being jolted out of place

parts.note: taken as written
one is I in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A shocking opening scene in a staging of Chekhov's play by a brother.
explanation.walkthrough: Chekhov's Three Sisters is a play; the question mark warns that the definition is read literally, as three girls a brother has produced.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's daughters are his siblings' nieces, so any sisters he fathers are nieces to them.

clue.text: Set out again from a dead-end street in need of repairs

indicators.note: in need of repairs implies the letters are broken and must be put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written
the end of the word dead is its last letter, D
taken as written

explanation.surface: A road out of a cul-de-sac needs repairing before it can be used again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in need of repairs' rearranges A, D and STREET.
explanation.definitionFit: To restate something is to set it out again in words.
